title_a: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
title_b: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
rationale: Both papers sit in the prompt-injection-on-RAG problem family, so failure type and broad threat space overlap. However, Paper A is an offensive contribution that backdoors the retriever (corpus/retriever-side training-time intervention) and reports attack success rate, while Paper B is a defensive contribution intervening at the generator/system-control layer with detection or mitigation metrics. Role asymmetry plus divergent intervention points and action policies preclude direct ranking, though they can be co-evaluated in a shared attack-defense harness as complementary mechanisms.

title_a: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
title_b: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
rationale: Both are attacker-side artifacts targeting retrieved content in RAG, so the adversarial family overlaps. However, ADMIT is a knowledge-poisoning method that injects false factual passages to flip fact-checking verdicts, while HiPT is a benchmark for indirect prompt injection where the payload is instructions hidden in social-web text. Failure semantics differ (content falsification vs instruction hijacking), the downstream task differs (fact-checking vs general RAG), and a method-vs-benchmark asymmetry blocks direct ranking. Comparable only after harmonizing payload type, task, and a shared attack-success metric.

title_a: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
title_b: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
rationale: Both papers occupy the RAG corpus-poisoning threat space, so failure type and broad evidence assumption overlap. However, ProGRank is a defender artifact intervening at retriever-side reranking with metrics on attack mitigation and a filter/rerank action, while Paper B is a vulnerability/attack study intervening at the corpus with attack-success-rate as the headline metric and no defender action policy. Role asymmetry (attack vs defense) and divergent interventions/actions preclude direct leaderboard ranking; they can only be reconciled inside a shared attack-defense harness with matched insertion budgets and a joint metric bundle.

title_a: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
title_b: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
rationale: The two papers diverge on every coordinate: Paper A is a defensive method against indirect prompt injection (instruction-following hijack via embedded directives) operating at the generator/context with detection-based filtering and reporting detection/ASR-reduction metrics, while Paper B is an offensive corpus-side knowledge poisoning attack specifically targeting graph-based RAG architectures and reporting attack success rate with no defender action policy. The failure types (instruction hijack vs knowledge graph corruption), RAG substrate (text vs graph), roles (defender vs attacker), and metrics are non-substitutable, so a direct leaderboard comparison would produce a category error rather than a meaningful ranking.

title_a: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
title_b: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
rationale: Both works sit in the same broad family of deciding when a RAG system should retrieve or abstain rather than answer from parametric memory. Paper A is a training-free method intervening at system control (uncertainty-triggered retrieval) and retriever (dual-path), optimizing answer correctness and retrieval cost. Paper B is an evaluation library that constructs out-of-KB testbeds and measures abstention/refusal and faithfulness. The method-vs-benchmark asymmetry plus different metric targets and partially overlapping action policies preclude direct ranking; Paper A could be evaluated on Paper B but they are not substitutable on a common leaderboard.

title_a: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
title_b: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
rationale: Both papers sit in the adaptive-retrieval-decision family: Paper A diagnoses over-searching (unnecessary retrieval calls by search-augmented LLMs) while Paper B uses pre-training-corpus uncertainty to trigger dynamic retrieval. The failure framings overlap on when-to-retrieve, but assumptions diverge (post-hoc search-behavior signal vs. pre-training-corpus uncertainty estimate) and interventions sit at different control points (suppressing redundant search vs. uncertainty-gated trigger). Metric emphasis likely differs (search-cost/over-search rate vs. accuracy-cost trade-off under dynamic triggering), so direct ranking would require a harmonized triggering policy and metric bundle.

title_a: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
title_b: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
rationale: Both papers address the trust/abstention family under uncertain RAG evidence and share an answer-or-abstain action policy, so they sit in the same problem family. However, Paper A targets KG-RAG with a causality-aware calibration framework (system-control/post-hoc trust scoring), while Paper B trains a textual-context generator via RL to ground or abstain. Evidence modality (structured KG vs textual passages), intervention point (calibration layer vs RL fine-tuning), and headline metric (calibration/accuracy vs groundedness/abstention quality) all diverge, so direct ranking would require harmonized interventions and a unified metric bundle.

title_a: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
title_b: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
rationale: Both works belong to the reliability/selective-generation family of RAG and both ultimately gate answering on a trust signal, so they overlap on failure framing (unreliable answers under imperfect retrieval) and on the abstain-vs-answer action axis. However, Paper A operationalizes failure as miscalibrated generator confidence and intervenes with a calibration-oriented training/decoding objective measured by calibration and selective-risk metrics, while Paper B reframes failure as insufficient retrieved context, intervenes via a sufficient-context classifier as a diagnostic lens plus selective generation, and reports hallucination and accuracy-coverage curves. Intervention point, primary metric target, and the trigger for abstention differ enough that direct ranking would require a harmonized selective-prediction protocol.

title_a: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
title_b: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
rationale: PrismRAG targets RAG factuality under retrieved distractor passages using a generator-side training method (distractor resilience plus strategized reasoning), while the second paper studies an inverse-scaling phenomenon for distractor instructions via the DistractionIF diagnostic. Both share a conceptual distractor-robustness theme, but the failure surface differs (noisy retrieved context vs. distractor instructions in the prompt), as do the intervention type (training method vs. benchmark/scaling analysis), the headline metric, and the system action (improved answer vs. measurement only), so direct ranking is not warranted.

title_a: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
title_b: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
rationale: Both papers address degradation of RAG generation quality from imperfect retrieved context on QA-style tasks, so they sit in the same problem family. However, the specific failure modes diverge: Paper A targets positional sensitivity / order bias ('lost in the middle') and intervenes at the generator via parallel KV-cache fusion to make answering position-invariant, whereas Paper B targets distraction by irrelevant passages and intervenes at the retriever by learning a distraction-aware selection policy, with an explicit efficiency/long-context trade-off metric Paper A does not report. Direct ranking would require harmonizing intervention point, action policy (process-all vs. selective retrieval), and the metric bundle (accuracy alone vs. accuracy+cost+context-length).

title_a: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
title_b: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
rationale: Both papers target the same failure family — generator distraction by irrelevant or distractor passages in RAG — and intervene generator-side, so they are clearly in the same problem family. However, the intervention mechanisms diverge sharply: entropy-based decoding is a training-free inference-time contrastive decoder, while RAFT is a domain-specific supervised fine-tuning recipe with chain-of-thought citation. Evidence assumption (general ODQA noise vs domain-specific distractor mixture), evaluation suites, and action policy (plain answer vs CoT-cited answer) also differ, so direct ranking would require a harmonized benchmark and matched action contract.

title_a: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
title_b: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
rationale: Both papers sit in the noisy-retrieval failure family for RAG and likely share answer-accuracy reporting, but they play different roles: Paper A is an empirical scaling study of how SLMs utilize retrieved evidence (diagnostic, no proposed mitigation), while Paper B (END) is a concrete intervention that drops noisy context early at the context-assembly/generator interface. Intervention point, action policy (measure vs filter), and metric focus (scale-conditioned utilization vs denoising gain plus efficiency) diverge, preventing direct ranking on a common leaderboard.

title_a: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
source_a: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025
title_b: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

Their evidence assumptions differ (gold references vs no-reference), their intervention scopes differ (dataset+metrics vs metric library), and the action is uniformly evaluate so no system policy is exercised. Direct ranking is inappropriate; they are complementary and would need a harmonized harness where RAGAs metrics are validated on MIRAGE data against MIRAGE metrics on shared RAG outputs.

title_a: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
source_a: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2024

Failure type, threat model, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge; they can be complementary diagnostics but cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard without harmonizing what is being measured and where.

title_a: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations

title_a: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
title_b: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models

Interventions sit at different stages (benchmark construction vs scoring), metrics differ (downstream robustness on leakage-free data vs judge-human agreement and self-consistency), and action policies diverge (produce evaluation data vs produce evaluation scores). Same family, not directly rankable; they are complementary infrastructure rather than substitutable methods.

title_a: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
title_b: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization

Intervention point, metric target, and action policy (pure answer-with-attribution vs summarize-then-answer) diverge, so they function as complementary rather than directly rankable.

title_a: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
title_b: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Direct ranking requires harmonizing the action contract (answer-faithful vs answer-faithful-with-conflict-trace) and matching backbones and faithfulness metric suites.

title_a: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators

The failure modes (pragmatic harm in a safety-critical domain vs. architectural attention bias), evidence assumptions, interventions, metrics, and action policies are all disjoint, so they do not share a problem family and direct ranking would be misleading.

title_a: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
title_b: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise

Paper B targets robustness to constructed counterfactual passages, with a different mitigation pathway and an action framed as resisting/ignoring counterfactual noise rather than explicit source arbitration. Construction protocols for conflict scenarios likely differ, breaking direct ranking.

title_a: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
title_b: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation

The failure modes (plan synthesis errors vs GFM knowledge gaps), intervention substrates (planner with verifier vs GFM augmentation), and action policies diverge entirely, making a direct leaderboard comparison structurally inappropriate.

title_a: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
title_b: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models

They do not share a robust-RAG failure mode, threat or noise assumption, intervention point, metric target, or action policy, so they cannot be placed on a common leaderboard and direct ranking would be misleading.

title_a: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
title_b: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation

Neither squarely targets robust-RAG noise, conflict, or adversarial failures; intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, so direct ranking is inappropriate.

title_a: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
title_b: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation

Intervention points also diverge (retriever ranking plus generator decoding vs context-assembly winnowing/filtering), and the implied action policies differ (rerank-then-answer vs filter-then-answer). Direct leaderboard ranking would require harmonized conflict-vs-noise slices and a matched action contract.

title_a: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
title_b: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
rationale: Both are RAG enhancement methods that intervene around the retriever-generator interface and report QA accuracy on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, etc.), so they share a problem family. However, RankRAG targets noisy/irrelevant retrieval via instruction-tuned context reranking (rank-then-answer), while xRAG targets context length and inference cost via projector-based single-token compression (compress-then-answer). The primary failure modes (retrieval noise vs context inefficiency) and metric targets (answer quality vs quality-efficiency tradeoff) differ, so a direct leaderboard would conflate solutions to different problems.

title_a: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
source_a: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title_a: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
title_b: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

title_a: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
title_b: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
rationale: Paper A is a comprehensive survey synthesizing architectures, enhancements, and robustness frontiers across all of RAG, with no single failure mode, intervention point, metric, or action policy of its own. Paper B is a denoising-first perspective focused specifically on retrieval-stage noise mitigation for LLM-oriented IR. A survey and a focused perspective/method piece cannot be placed on a common leaderboard because the survey produces no comparable experimental results and spans a superset of the coordinates that Paper B narrowly addresses. The role asymmetry (synthesis vs. contribution) is structural, not fixable by harmonization.

title_a: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
title_b: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
rationale: Both works are surveys of trustworthy RAG and share the broad problem family, with substantial overlap in covered failure modes (hallucination, conflict, poisoning, privacy, fairness). However, surveys do not produce a single rankable result; they organize the literature under different taxonomies and emphasize different intervention points, metric bundles, and recommended action policies. Direct comparability would require harmonizing their dimension schemas and the per-dimension scope they each cover, so they are complementary references rather than head-to-head comparables.

title_a: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
title_b: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
rationale: Paper A is a security-focused taxonomy of RAG attacks and defenses (failure = adversarial integrity/availability threats; metrics = attack success rate, defense efficacy; actions = filter/quarantine/verify), while Paper B (RAPID) is an inference-efficiency contribution applying retrieval-augmented speculative decoding to long-context generation (failure = latency/throughput under long contexts; metric = speedup with quality preservation; action = accelerated generation). The two works share no failure mode, threat model, intervention point, metric target, or action policy — they live in disjoint problem families (security vs. inference efficiency) and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.

title_a: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
title_b: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
rationale: Structural role asymmetry mirrors the P08 pattern: PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-injection attack reporting attack success rate with no defender action, while Trust-or-Abstain is a defensive generator-side self-awareness method whose action policy is answer-vs-abstain under uncertainty, almost certainly framed around benign retrieval unreliability rather than an explicit adversarial threat model. Without a shared attack-defense harness fixing insertion budget, retriever, and metric bundle (ASR plus selective risk), direct ranking would conflate distinct failure modes and produce misleading conclusions.

title_a: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
title_b: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis

The axiomatic UE paper targets a fundamentally different failure mode, namely miscalibrated uncertainty estimation of RAG outputs, with axiomatic/calibration-quality metrics and an abstain/confidence-style action policy. Failure type, metric target, and action policy all diverge; placing them on a shared leaderboard would conflate noise-robustness benchmarking with UE diagnosis and yield misleading conclusions.

title_a: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
title_b: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization

title_a: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
title_b: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
rationale: Paper A targets complex hierarchical task planning failures over structured knowledge graphs with symbolic verification of plan steps, while Paper B targets unsupportive or noisy passages in standard text-RAG QA via a learned rewriter. Failure modes (plan-step infeasibility vs unsupportive evidence), evidence assumptions (KG triples vs free-text passages), intervention surfaces (symbolic verifier in a planner loop vs context rewriting), metrics (task/plan success vs answer accuracy), and actions (verify-and-replan vs rewrite-then-answer) all diverge, so a direct ranking would conflate different problems.

title_a: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
title_b: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
rationale: Paper A is an offensive study of indirect prompt injection delivered via retrieved content, with an adversarial threat model and attack-success framing at the corpus/retrieval boundary. Paper B is a defensive RL method that trains a generator to ground responses and abstain under contextual evidence, with no explicit adversarial threat model and metrics centered on grounding and selective answering. Roles, threat models, intervention points, metrics, and action policies all diverge, so direct ranking would mislead; only a shared attack-defense harness could bridge them.

title_a: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
title_b: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems

They share the broader robust-RAG family and overlap on context-level intervention, so partial fits better than invalid, but metrics (conflict handling/faithfulness vs attack success/clean accuracy) and action policies (cite-both/abstain vs filter/quarantine) preclude head-to-head comparison.

title_a: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
title_b: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
rationale: Both papers sit under the broad robust-RAG umbrella but address distinct sub-problems: RoseRAG targets noise robustness of small-scale generators via margin-aware preference optimization, with an answer-generation action and EM/F1-style accuracy metrics. Paper B targets faithfulness/hallucination detection via post-hoc uncertainty quantification, with a verify/flag action and calibration/fact-checking metrics. title_a: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
title_b: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling

Failure modes (table retrieval mismatch vs noisy/irrelevant sentences), assumption (structured tables vs free-text passages), interventions (retriever scoring vs post-retrieval refinement), and benchmarks differ, so they share an action (answer) and a family goal but cannot be directly ranked.

title_a: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
title_b: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
rationale: TrustRAG targets adversarial corpus poisoning under a malicious threat model and intervenes via trust/filter mechanisms with metrics like attack success rate and robust accuracy. SUGAR addresses when to retrieve at all, using contextual confidence to gate retrieval under benign assumptions, with metrics on answer accuracy and retrieval cost. Different failure types, threat models, intervention points, metric targets, and action policies; placing them on a common leaderboard would conflate security defense with adaptive-retrieval efficiency.

title_a: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts
title_b: GraphRAG under Fire
